title: Google’s AI note-taking app now allows you to interact with books
slides: It now lets you chat with uploaded books.
But it misquotes when pages exceed 500.
Your workflow shifts from skimming to interrogation.
Test it on one book before trusting summaries.
thread_text:
1. Chat with your books now

Google's NotebookLM lets you ask questions directly to uploaded books, turning static PDFs into conversational partners.

2. But 500 pages breaks it

When books exceed 500 pages, the tool starts misquoting. Your source becomes a gaslighter.

3. Skimming is dead

Your workflow shifts from skimming to interrogation. You're not reading—you're cross-examining text.

4. Trust but verify

Misquotations mean you can't trust summaries blindly. Verification becomes part of the job.

5. Test it before you rely

Put one book through NotebookLM this week. Does it hold up? If not, keep your highlighter.

script: Upload a book, chat with it.

instagram.caption:
You can now interrogate a book instead of reading it. Google’s NotebookLM lets you upload a PDF and chat with it like a source.

But push past 500 pages and it starts making things up. Misquotations appear, meaning the tool quietly fabricates lines that aren't in the text. Your skim-and-highlight workflow becomes cross-examination mode: you ask, it answers, and you verify everything.

For anyone writing summaries or citing sources, this changes the trust equation. You can’t delegate comprehension to a chat window when the quotes might be invented.

Test one book under 500 pages this week before you rely on it for anything you publish. Does the trade-off feel worth it to you? 📚🔍🧠
